chapters.relation: The concluding chapter argues that Joss Whedon 'does philosophy' on television, not merely illustrates it, by ranking degrees of filmic philosophizing (via Wartenberg, Shaw, Mulhall) and showing the Whedenverse meets them. It reads Angel/Angelus and Fred/Illyria as cinematic thought experiments that generate 'metaphysical complexity' about personal identity, playing memory- and continuity-of-consciousness theories (Locke, Parfit) against a soul theory, and reads Connor's origin as exemplifying Kane's libertarian free will. It contends Whedon endorses a Noddings-style ethics of care and an existentialist yet God-independent morality, epitomized by Angel's 'Epiphany' speech ('the smallest act of kindness is the greatest thing') and 'Deep Down,' plus the 'Man on the Street' Academic monologue, staging a negative project against the claim that ethics is incoherent without God through the self-sacrifices of Simon, Cordelia, and Buffy.
